Range & clock

From the figure to the physics

Fig. 1 shows how one receiver clock offset enters every satellite pseudorange measurement.

A simplified pseudorange is ρᵢ = ‖r − rᵢ‖ + cb + error, where r is receiver position, rᵢ is known satellite position, and b is receiver clock bias in seconds.

The same receiver-clock bias adds a common distance term cb to every measurement. Subtracting a guessed correction changes all corresponding range-circle or range-sphere radii together.

A normal three-dimensional solution has four unknowns: three position coordinates and one clock bias. Four independent measurements supply the minimum count; satellite-clock and propagation corrections belong in a fuller observation model.

Example

A receiver clock bias of 1 μs contributes approximately 299.8 m to every pseudorange. That common term can greatly exceed the desired position precision.

Model and course sources

    Practice

    1. Why are three pseudoranges generally insufficient for a three-dimensional position when receiver time is also unknown?

    Count scalar unknowns before counting equations.

    There are four unknowns: x, y, z, and b. Three equations need an additional constraint or known quantity, such as a known height or independently known receiver time.
